# Ledger Process #

## Introduction ##

## Life Cycle ##

Every server always has an open ledger. All received new transactions are applied to the open ledger. The open ledger can't close until we reach a consensus on the previous ledger, and either: there is at least one transaction in the open ledger, or the ledger's close time has been reached.

When the open ledger is closed the transactions in the open ledger become the initial proposal. Validators will send the proposal (non-validators will simply not send the proposal). The open ledger contains the set of transactions the server thinks should go into the next ledger.

The most recent ledger that the server believes the network reached consensus on. Different servers can arrive at a different conclusion about the last closed ledger. This is a consequence of Byzantanine failure. The purpose of validations is to resolve the differences between servers and come to a common conclusion about which last closed ledger is authoritative.

## Consensus ##

A distributed agreement protocol. Ripple uses the consensus process to solve the problem of double-spending.

## Validation ##

A signed statement indicating that it built a particular ledger as a result of the consensus process.

## Proposal ##

A signed statement of which transactions it believes should be included in the next consensus ledger.

## Ledger Header ##

The "ledger header" is the chunk of data that hashes to the ledger's hash. It contains the sequence number, parent hash, hash of the previous ledger, hash of the root node of the state tree, and so on.

# NodeStore

## Introduction

A `NodeObject` is a simple object that the Ledger uses to store entries. It is comprised of a type, a hash and a blob. It can be uniquely identified by the hash, which is a 256 bit hash of the blob. The blob is a variable length block of serialized data. The type identifies what the blob contains. The fields are as follows:

`mType`

An enumeration that determines what the blob holds. There are four different types of objects stored.

**ledger**

A ledger header.

**transaction**

A signed transaction.

**account node**

A node in a ledger's account state tree.

**transaction node**

A node in a ledger's transaction tree.

`mHash`

A 256-bit hash of the blob.

`mData`

A blob containing the payload. Stored in the following format.

If we need either of those two ledgers they are fetched with the highest priority.  Also, when they arrive, they replace their earlier counterparts (if they exist).

The `LedgerMaster` object tracks - the last published ledger, - the last validated ledger, and - ledger history. So the `LedgerMaster` is at the center of fetching historical ledger data.

In specific, the `LedgerMaster::doAdvance()` method triggers the code that fetches historical data and controls the state machine for ledger acquisition.

The server tries to publish an on-going stream of consecutive ledgers to its clients.  After the server has started and caught up with network activity, say when ledger 500 is being settled, then the server puts its best effort into publishing validated ledger 500 followed by validated ledger 501 and then 502.  This effort continues until the server is shut down.

Byzantine failures are resolved as follows. If there is a supermajority ledger, then a minority of validators will discover that the consensus round is proceeding on a different ledger than they thought. These validators will become desynced, and switch to a strategy of trying to acquire the consensus ledger.

If there is no majority ledger, then starting on the next consensus round there will not be a consensus on the last closed ledger. Another avalanche process is started.

## Validators ##

The only meaningful difference between a validator and a 'regular' server is that the validator sends its proposals and validations to the network.

--

# The Ledger Stream #

## Ledger Priorities ##

There are two ledgers that are the most important for a rippled server to have:

The consensus ledger and

The last validated ledger.

When data for a ledger arrives from a peer, it may take a while before the server can apply that data.  So when ledger data arrives we schedule a job thread to apply that data.  If more data arrives before the job starts we add that data to the job.  We defer requesting more ledger data until all of the data we have for that ledger has been processed.  Once all of that data is processed we can intelligently request only the additional data that we need to fill in the ledger.  This reduces network traffic and minimizes the load on peers supplying the data.

If we receive data for a ledger that is not currently under construction, we don't just throw the data away.  In particular the AccountStateNodes may be useful, since they can be re-used across ledgers.  This data is stashed in memory (not the database) where the acquire process can find it.

ai.description: This file defines the LedgerHolder class, which manages a thread-safe, immutable shared pointer to a Ledger object. It provides methods to set a new immutable ledger, retrieve the current ledger, and check if a ledger is held. The class uses a mutex to ensure thread safety and enforces that only immutable ledgers can be set, throwing logic errors otherwise.

This file implements the PeerImp class, which represents a peer connection in the XRPL (Ripple) overlay network. PeerImp manages the lifecycle and communication of a peer, including connection setup, message sending and receiving, protocol negotiation, resource usage tracking, and feature support. It handles various protocol messages (transactions, validations, proposals, ledger data, etc.), manages transaction and ledger queues, enforces resource limits, and supports features like transaction reduce-relay, ledger replay, and squelching. The class also tracks peer metrics (latency, bytes sent/received), manages peer status and tracking (converged/diverged), and interacts with other network components such as the job queue, ledger master, validators, and resource manager. The file includes logic for relaying messages, handling protocol errors, charging peers for resource usage, and maintaining peer state for network health and synchronization.

This file implements the InboundLedgersImp class, which manages the acquisition and tracking of inbound ledgers in the Ripple (XRPL) server. It handles requests to acquire ledgers from the network, manages ongoing acquisitions, tracks failures, and processes incoming ledger data from peers. The class provides methods to acquire ledgers synchronously and asynchronously, check for failures, process stale data, clear caches, and report status information. It uses mutexes for thread safety and maintains internal maps for active acquisitions and recent failures. The file also includes a factory function to create instances of InboundLedgersImp. The overall design ensures efficient and robust management of ledger data needed for consensus and network operations.

This file implements functions to serialize ledger data structures into JSON format for the XRPL (XRP Ledger) server. It provides utilities to convert ledger information, transactions, account states, and transaction queues into various JSON representations, supporting different output options such as full, expanded, or binary formats. The code is designed to support the needs of the XRPL API, including backward compatibility and detailed transaction metadata.

ai.description: This file defines the core logic for the consensus process in the Ripple (XRPL) ledger system. It provides a highly generic, template-based Consensus class that manages the state and progression of consensus rounds among network peers. The class is parameterized by an Adaptor, allowing it to be used with different ledger and transaction set types. The consensus process involves collecting proposals from peers, tracking their positions, managing disputes over transactions, and determining when consensus has been reached or failed. The class handles transitions between different consensus phases (open, establish, accepted), manages timing and round progression, and provides mechanisms for pausing, simulating, and forcibly accepting consensus. It also includes logic for handling peers that fall out of sync, managing close times, and updating the local node's position based on peer input. The file includes utility functions for determining when to close a ledger, checking for consensus, and serializing the consensus state to JSON for monitoring or debugging. The MonitoredMode inner class tracks and manages the current consensus mode (proposing, observing, wrong ledger, etc.), ensuring the Adaptor is notified of mode changes. Overall, this file encapsulates the state machine and algorithms required for distributed agreement on ledger state in the XRPL network.

This file implements the LedgerCleaner component for the XRPL (Ripple) server. The main class, LedgerCleanerImp, manages a background thread that cleans and repairs ledger data within a specified range. It can check for missing or inconsistent ledger nodes and transactions, and attempts to fix them by reacquiring or saving ledgers as needed. The class supports starting and stopping the cleaning process, configuring the cleaning range and options via JSON parameters, and reporting its status. The cleaning process is careful to avoid running during high server load and tracks failures, retrying as necessary. The file also provides a factory function to create instances of the LedgerCleaner.
